narrative:
Over the past 12 days a single campaign accounted for 275 sessions originating from 73 source IPs across 35 countries and 57 ASNs. Every session followed the same short sequence: append an attacker-controlled RSA public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, set the immutable bit on the file with chattr +i, and add a crontab entry that re-runs the installer every five minutes.

The behaviour is consistent with persistent SSH access intended to survive a defender removing the authorized_keys file: the immutable bit blocks ordinary removal until chattr -i is run first, and the cron job re-installs the key once it disappears. The geographic spread (35 countries, 57 ASNs) plus the identical command sequence across every session reads as a botnet rather than a single actor — the same RSA key (sha256:c2c1e9557c5abc30...ae6cbb57) appears across all 73 IPs, tying the operator behind them.

Confidence is moderate. The behavioural fingerprint is distinctive and the cross-IP consistency strong, but external intel verdicts have only landed on 3 of the 73 IPs (all malicious). A second cycle confirming the same membership, or a community signal on the remaining 70 IPs, would push this to high confidence; an absence of either over the next week would suggest the campaign is winding down.

For defenders: the immutable-bit step is the auditable tell. chattr +i on a file under ~/.ssh is rare in legitimate operations — a single hunt across SSH-exposed hosts (lsattr ~/.ssh/authorized_keys) catches this regardless of whether the key was rotated.
